etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English entertenen, from Middle French entretenir, from Old French entretenir, from entre (“among”) + tenir (“to hold”), from Latin inter + teneō (“hold, keep”). For the noun, compare French entretien.

definitions.definition: (transitive) to amuse (someone); to engage the attention of agreeably
(transitive and intransitive) to have someone over at one's home for a party or visit

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Hebrews 13:2:
quote.text: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) to receive and take into consideration; to have a thought in mind

quote.text: I am not here going to entertain so large a theme as the philosophy of Locke.

quote.citation: 1850, Nathaniel Hawthorne, The Scarlet Letter, a Romance, Boston, Mass.: Ticknor, Reed, and Fields, →OCLC:
quote.text: A rumour gained ground, — and, however absurd, was entertained by some very sensible people.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) to take or keep in one's service; to maintain; to support; to harbour; to keep

quote.citation: c. 1589–1590 (date written), Christopher Marlo[we], edited by Tho[mas] Heywood, The Famous Tragedy of the Rich Iew of Malta. […], London:  […]  I[ohn] B[eale] for Nicholas Vavasour, […], published 1633, →OCLC, Act I:
quote.text: Intreat 'em fair, and give them friendly speech,And seem to them as if thy sins were great,Till thou hast gotten to be entertain'd.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act XXVI, scene iii], page vi:
quote.text: You, sir, I entertain for one of my hundred.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) to meet or encounter, as an enemy

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: O noble English, that could entertain with half their forces the full pride of France

quote.citation: 1860, British Parliament, Naval Discipline Act‎[1], page 1069:

definitions.definition: (obsolete) to lead on; to bring along; to introduce

quote.citation: 1651–1653, Jer[emy] Taylor, ΕΝΙΑΥΤΟΣ [Eniautos]. A Course of Sermons for All the Sundays of the Year. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  Richard Royston […], published 1655, →OCLC:
quote.text: to baptize all nations, and to entertain them into the services and institutions of the holy Jesus

quote.citation: c. 1603 (date written), Iohn Marston, The Malcontent, London:  […]  V[alentine] S[immes] for William Aspley, […], published 1604, →OCLC, Act V, scene iii:
quote.text: And Celſo, prethee let it be thy care to night / To haue ſome pretty ſhew, to ſolemnize / Our high inſtalement, ſome muſike maſkerie: / Weele giue faire entertaine vnto Maria  […]

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book IV, Canto VIII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
